summary: A 1976 proposal for the Message Services Data Transmission Protocol, a mechanism for message servers to move data between hosts. It treats the process as a translation between abstract items such as strings and integers and the byte formats that represent them.

plainLanguage.summary: MSDTP describes how a sending program can turn data such as numbers and text into bytes, then let another program rebuild the data. It separates what the data means from how each computer stores it.

subtitle: A byte-stream format for moving typed data between message servers on different hosts.

tldr.problem: Message servers need to exchange structured data even when hosts represent values differently.
tldr.mechanism: MSDTP defines abstract items, byte-stream objects, and translation rules between them.
tldr.outcome: The document also sketches a broader transfer system using different translators for different media.

today: The unit metadata gives RFC 713 an Unknown status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Items and Their Encodings
sections.content:
MSDTP models data as abstract items, including integers, strings, structures, bit streams, characters, booleans, empty values, and application-defined semantic items. An item is translated into an encoded object, sent as a byte stream, and reconstructed at the receiving host.

This lets applications describe exchanges in terms of items rather than local memory formats. The RFC is written for message servers using an eight-bit byte-oriented connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A program describes the value it wants to send. MSDTP turns that value into bytes and gives the receiver rules for rebuilding it.

sections.title: Primitive, Semantic, and Byte-Stream Forms
sections.content:
Primitive items cover common values such as integers and strings. A semantic item adds application-specific meaning through an extended data type with a type identifier and a version number. The RFC gives a file specification as an example of such a type.

Every encoded object begins with a type byte. Atomic objects compactly represent common values; non-atomic objects carry larger or less common values with size information. Structures can contain other encoded objects, and repeat objects can represent repeated patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic vocabulary handles common values. Applications can add named, versioned values, while the byte format marks each object so a receiver can decode it.

sections.title: Using Translators for Different Media
sections.content:
The final section proposes a wider data-transfer environment. Programs would define their exchanges using shared primitive items, while a set of translators would convert those items for available communication media.

The proposal notes that a translator may not support every item and that efficiency can vary by medium. A separate, not-yet-defined protocol would let the communicating modules match capabilities and select a medium and translator.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications could use one vocabulary while separate translators adapt the data to each connection type. The RFC presents this wider arrangement as a proposal.

references.text: Myer, T. H., and D. A. Henderson, "Message Transmission Protocol", RFC 680, April 1975.
